$comment: Coverage map: every entry in runtime/skills/ (each directory, including the design symlink) and runtime/agents/ (each .md file) appears exactly once. books: [] is an explicit decision that no vendored rule book changes that entry's decisions — absence is a decision, not an omission. defaultTier is the no-budget-info fallback (usually mini; nano for entries that run on tight/fast lanes). Hosts and routers may pick a different tier from the target lane's context window; treat defaultTier as a recommendation, consistent with the headless contract. Enforced by scripts/check-rules-coverage.mjs (npm run rules:check).

books.why: Regression benchmarking decisions (what to measure, percentiles, load realism) are DDIA's core territory.
Characterization-before-change and seam-finding discipline matches the skill's iron law of investigation before fixes.
Production release gates, stability patterns, and failure-mode thinking are Release It!'s subject.

Dig-for-real-requirements, tracer bullets, and prototype honesty rule on the decisions this interview actually makes: whether an answer is a durable need or a restated solution, and whether the wedge is one thin end-to-end slice or a pile of disconnected pieces. Replaces domain-driven-design-distilled, whose Core/Supporting/Generic subdomain split was the only one of its 16 decision rules with a decision point in a file that has no code and no model — the remaining 15 are aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, context mapping, and integration styles.
Rollback triggers and stability signals from Release It!; nano because the canary loop runs on a tight monitoring cadence with little context to spare.
Post-deploy verification, canary rollout, and failure response map directly to Release It!'s operations rules.
Delegating work across heterogeneous lanes is a distributed-systems trade-off problem; DDIA's rules about partitioning, latency, and failure domains apply.
Deep modules, information hiding, and complexity budgets are the vocabulary this skill's decision sections need.
Dependency direction and boundary placement complement APoSD at the system-structure level (complementary per upstream matrix).
The engineering review lens of the planning gauntlet needs broad engineering judgment, not the code-level smell catalog the seed suggested (Refactoring); this skill reviews plans, not code.

Narrow but real: applies at Step 3 (component library) and the audit's consistency check only, where a component's props and variants are a module interface and APoSD's deep-module, small-surface, and no-knobs rules decide whether a fifth variant is a distinction or a configuration knob. The rest of the skill — design tokens, WCAG 2.1 AA criteria, style-guide writing — is outside the book's subject, and the instruction in the skill says so, so a token- or accessibility-only lane can skip it knowingly. Kept rather than emptied because no vendored book covers visual design or accessibility, and clean-code (overlapping — pick one) is strictly worse on interface design.
Tracer-bullet and orthogonality rules are what make a locked mechanism contract falsifiable: one thin end-to-end change, and the verifier stays a separate surface.
Scoping a feature spec benefits from bounded-context and ubiquitous-language discipline; the distilled variant is the single DDD book vendored.
Code-smell vocabulary and safe-change discipline back the review's defect hunting; chosen over refactoring-guru (overlapping — pick one) for its judgment rules rather than transform catalog.
Behavior-preserving migration of an existing app is the legacy-code problem: characterization tests before change.
Mechanical transform catalog for the long non-stop rewrite loop; nano keeps it cheap inside an already context-heavy run. Complementary with WELC per upstream matrix.
Transparency and monitoring-as-a-feature rules define what an observability foundation must expose.
Construction-quality and testing chapters cover journey validation and defect triage; chosen over clean-code (overlapping — pick one) for its broader testing coverage.
Failure-aware system design needs APoSD's complexity and deep-module rules.
Boundary and dependency-direction rules complement APoSD for system-level plans (complementary per upstream matrix).
Primary execution agent writing code benefits from naming/function/size rules; chosen over code-complete (overlapping — pick one) as the tighter code-writing rule set.
Decision-grade architecture and risk plans lean on APoSD's strategic-vs-tactical programming and complexity rules.
Broad execution judgment (tracer bullets, good-enough software, DRY) for the plan-exec wrapper, per seed mapping.
Fast lane for small obvious tasks; nano because this lane runs with minimal steps and tight context. Chosen over code-complete (overlapping — pick one).
Triage, containment, and rollback coordination is Release It!'s stability and recovery territory.
Same broad execution judgment as execution-orchestrator; nano because the parallel wrapper already carries plan payload plus per-slice state in context.
Regression detection and cost/perf trade-offs draw on DDIA's measurement and scalability rules.
Broad default for the primary planning agent, per seed mapping.
Journey validation and regression-risk judgment backed by Code Complete's quality and testing rules; chosen over clean-code (overlapping — pick one).
Lower-latency reasoning lane; nano fits the tight context budget this lane exists for.
CI enforcement, deploy gates, and post-deploy verification are Release It!'s core rules.

Blast-radius mapping is WELC's effect-tracing rule under another name — trace effects outward from the change point through values, calls, fields, outputs, collaborators, interception points, and pinch points — and its legacy-risk list gives read-only findings a vocabulary for which risks are worth reporting. Replaces the-pragmatic-programmer, whose own why admitted it was a broad seed default: this agent never writes code, and TPP's applicable content was two coupling rules plus a restatement of the agent's existing citation rule. Same book as debug-investigate, for the same investigate-before-change reason.
Code-smell vocabulary and safe-change judgment for pre-merge review; chosen over refactoring-guru (overlapping — pick one).
Full one-shot rewrites of existing apps are the legacy-code problem: characterize behavior before changing it.
Transform catalog for the compile/test repair loop; nano keeps it cheap in a 40-step context-heavy run. Complementary with WELC per upstream matrix.
